lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus: Type 1 versus Type 2, Complications and Diabetic Ketoacidosis

blocks.text: A 55-year-old bus driver goes to his general practitioner because a blister on his heel has not healed for two months and he has not felt the shoe rubbing for years. His feet are numb, his eyes have felt blurry, and his urine has been foamy. A fasting glucose is far above normal. Years of unnoticed hyperglycaemia have been quietly damaging his nerves, small vessels and kidneys.

blocks.markdown: **Diabetes mellitus** is a group of metabolic disorders characterised by chronic hyperglycaemia from deficient insulin secretion, insulin action, or both. Insulin, secreted by pancreatic **beta cells**, lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake into muscle and fat, glycogen synthesis, and suppression of hepatic glucose output and of lipolysis. Hyperglycaemia exceeds the renal threshold for glucose reabsorption, so glucose spills into urine and drags water with it (osmotic diuresis), producing **polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss**.

### Type 1 and type 2 diabetes

**Type 1 diabetes** is autoimmune destruction of beta cells. In genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DR3 and DR4 associations) a T-cell mediated insulitis destroys beta cells, and islet autoantibodies (for example against glutamic acid decarboxylase, GAD) are present. The result is **absolute insulin deficiency**. It usually presents in childhood or young adulthood with rapid onset, weight loss and a tendency to ketosis, and patients are dependent on insulin.

**Type 2 diabetes** is the commonest form and combines **insulin resistance** (reduced response of muscle, liver and fat, strongly related to obesity and visceral fat) with progressive **beta-cell dysfunction** that cannot sustain the compensatory hyperinsulinaemia. Pancreatic islets show amyloid deposition (islet amyloid polypeptide). It usually presents in adults, with insidious onset, often asymptomatic for years, and a strong family history; ketosis is unusual.

rows: Autoimmune beta cell destruction; absolute insulin deficiency
Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency and beta cell failure
Child or young adult; usually lean
Adult; usually overweight or obese (increasingly younger)
Lifestyle, oral agents, and insulin as needed

blocks.title: Diagnostic criteria
blocks.text: Common criteria (guidelines vary) are fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more, a random or 2-hour post-glucose-load value of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more, or HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more. In a patient without symptoms the abnormality should be confirmed on a second occasion.

blocks.caption: Approximate conversion between the two common units of blood glucose.

blocks.title: Applying the diagnostic threshold
blocks.prompt: An asymptomatic 49-year-old has a fasting plasma glucose of 140 mg/dL. Does this meet the diagnostic threshold for diabetes?

steps.text: The threshold for fasting glucose is 7.0 mmol/L, and 7.8 exceeds it.
Because he is asymptomatic, the diagnosis needs confirmation with a repeat test or another criterion.

blocks.answer: 7.8 mmol/L exceeds 7.0, so it is in the diabetic range, pending confirmation.

blocks.markdown:
### Complications

Chronic hyperglycaemia damages vessels through several routes: **advanced glycation end-products** that cross-link proteins, increased flux through the **polyol (sorbitol) pathway**, oxidative stress, and endothelial dysfunction. Complications are grouped by vessel size. **Microvascular** disease causes **retinopathy** (microaneurysms, haemorrhages, new vessels, blindness), **nephropathy** (basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion and Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, starting with microalbuminuria and progressing to renal failure) and **neuropathy** (symmetrical distal sensory loss, autonomic dysfunction). **Macrovascular** disease is accelerated atherosclerosis: ischaemic heart disease, stroke and peripheral arterial disease, and with neuropathy leads to diabetic foot ulcers and amputation.

rows: Capillary microaneurysms, leakage, ischaemia and neovascularisation
Glomerular basement membrane thickening, Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, albuminuria
Polyol pathway and vasa nervorum ischaemia; glove-and-stocking sensory loss
blocks.caption: Complications of diabetes
Albumin to creatinine ratio used to detect diabetic nephropathy: about 3 to 30 mg/mmol is moderately increased (microalbuminuria).

blocks.markdown:
### Diabetic ketoacidosis

**Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)**, mainly in type 1 diabetes, is a life-threatening emergency of **severe insulin deficiency with excess counter-regulatory hormones** (glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, growth hormone), often precipitated by infection, missed insulin or new-onset disease. Without insulin, adipose tissue releases free fatty acids by unrestrained lipolysis, and the liver converts them to **ketone bodies** (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate), which are acids, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Hyperglycaemia causes an osmotic diuresis with severe volume depletion. Total body potassium is depleted by urinary loss, although the measured serum level may be normal or high because acidosis and insulin lack shift potassium out of cells. Features are deep, sighing (Kussmaul) breathing that blows off CO2, a fruity odour of acetone, abdominal pain, vomiting and dehydration. Typical criteria combine hyperglycaemia (or known diabetes), ketonaemia and acidosis (pH below 7.3 or low bicarbonate).

blocks.title: Recognising DKA from the results
blocks.prompt: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has glucose 24 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.6 mmol/L, pH 7.10 and bicarbonate 8 mmol/L. Is this DKA, and what are the priorities of initial management?

steps.text: Hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia (about 3 mmol/L or above) and acidaemia with low bicarbonate meet the criteria for DKA.
The first priority is restoring volume with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride, since the deficit is large and fluid also lowers glucose and counter-regulatory hormones.

A fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion then switches off ketone production. Potassium is replaced according to monitored levels because insulin drives potassium into cells. The precipitant (infection, missed insulin) must be sought and treated.

blocks.answer: DKA; initial management is intravenous fluid, intravenous insulin infusion, potassium monitoring and replacement, and treatment of the precipitant (specific regimens are guideline-based).

points: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune beta cell destruction with absolute insulin deficiency; type 2 diabetes combines insulin resistance with relative beta cell failure.
Microvascular complications are retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy, and macrovascular complications are coronary, cerebral and peripheral atherosclerosis, all driven by chronic hyperglycaemia.
DKA results from severe insulin deficiency, with lipolysis and ketogenesis causing acidosis, and is managed with fluids, insulin, potassium and treatment of the cause.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old lean boy has had 3 weeks of thirst, polyuria and weight loss, with a random glucose of 26 mmol/L and positive anti-GAD antibodies. What is the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Autoimmune T-cell mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells
Insulin resistance of skeletal muscle with islet amyloid
Excess cortisol causing gluconeogenesis
Destruction of alpha cells

questions.correctOptionText: Autoimmune T-cell mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells

distractorRationale.a: Correct: islet autoantibodies and rapid onset in a lean adolescent indicate type 1 diabetes with beta cell destruction.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: insulin resistance with amyloid characterises type 2 diabetes.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: Cushing syndrome does not explain autoantibodies or this age and presentation.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: alpha cells make glucagon and are not the target.

questions.explanation: Rapid onset in a lean young person with islet autoantibodies is typical of autoimmune type 1 diabetes. Loss of beta cells causes absolute insulin deficiency, so treatment is with insulin.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Insulin resistance with progressive beta cell dysfunction that eventually cannot compensate
Complete autoimmune loss of beta cells with ketosis proneness
Isolated defect in renal glucose reabsorption
Primary excess of glucagon from alpha cells

questions.correctOptionText: Insulin resistance with progressive beta cell dysfunction that eventually cannot compensate

distractorRationale.a: Correct: type 2 diabetes results from resistance to insulin and failure of beta cell compensation, with islet amyloid.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: renal glycosuria does not cause hyperglycaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: glucagon excess is not the primary cause.

questions.explanation: Obesity-related insulin resistance forces beta cells to secrete more insulin, and over time they fail. The result is relative insulin deficiency with hyperglycaemia, and without the immune destruction of type 1.

questions.stem: A renal biopsy from a 58-year-old man with 20 years of diabetes shows nodular mesangial sclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules) and thickened glomerular basement membranes. Which category of complication does this represent?

options.text: Microvascular complication
Macrovascular complication
Acute metabolic complication
Infective complication

distractorRationale.a: Correct: diabetic nephropathy is damage to the small vessels of the glomerulus.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: macrovascular disease means atherosclerosis of large and medium arteries.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: acute metabolic complications include DKA and hypoglycaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is not an infection.

questions.explanation: Hyperglycaemia thickens the glomerular basement membrane and expands the mesangium, forming nodules. This is one of the classic microvascular complications along with retinopathy and neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes develops intermittent claudication, and then rest pain in a cold foot with absent pedal pulses. Which description is correct?

options.text: Macrovascular disease (accelerated atherosclerosis), compounded by neuropathy
Microvascular disease only
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Autoimmune vasculitis unrelated to diabetes

questions.correctOptionText: Macrovascular disease (accelerated atherosclerosis), compounded by neuropathy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: diabetes accelerates atherosclerosis of larger arteries, and neuropathy often coexists, increasing the risk of foot ulceration.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: absent pedal pulses indicate large-vessel disease.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: DKA is an acute metabolic emergency.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: there is no feature suggesting vasculitis.

questions.explanation: Diabetes accelerates atherosclerosis in large and medium arteries, producing peripheral arterial disease. Loss of pain sensation from neuropathy lets minor injuries progress to ulcers.

questions.stem: Why do ketone bodies accumulate in diabetic ketoacidosis?

options.text: Severe insulin deficiency causes unrestrained lipolysis, and the liver converts the fatty acids to ketones
Excess insulin causes hepatic fat synthesis
Renal failure prevents ketone excretion as the primary event
Dietary carbohydrate overload directly produces ketones

questions.correctOptionText: Severe insulin deficiency causes unrestrained lipolysis, and the liver converts the fatty acids to ketones

distractorRationale.a: Correct: absence of insulin removes the brake on lipolysis, and with high glucagon, hepatic ketogenesis is activated.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: renal impairment is not the cause of ketone formation.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: carbohydrate excess does not make ketones; lack of insulin action does.

questions.explanation: Insulin normally inhibits lipolysis and ketogenesis. In its absence, free fatty acids flood the liver and are converted to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, which are acids, causing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A patient presenting with abdominal pain and vomiting has a capillary glucose of 360 mg/dL. Convert this to mmol/L by dividing by 18.
questions.explanation: 360 / 18 = 20 mmol/L, well above the 11 mmol/L level typically used in the diagnostic criteria for DKA. Glucose alone does not confirm DKA, and ketones and acidosis must also be shown.

questions.stem: A man with type 2 diabetes has a spot urine albumin of 45 mg/L and urine creatinine of 7.5 mmol/L. Calculate the albumin to creatinine ratio (ACR) in mg/mmol.
questions.explanation: ACR = 45 / 7.5 = 6 mg/mmol. This lies in the range of about 3-30 mg/mmol that indicates moderately increased albuminuria, an early marker of diabetic nephropathy.

questions.stem: Contrast the pathogenesis, typical presentation and treatment needs of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
markingGuide: Type 1: autoimmune T-cell destruction of beta cells, islet autoantibodies, HLA association, absolute insulin deficiency
Type 2: insulin resistance with beta cell dysfunction, obesity, islet amyloid, relative insulin deficiency
Type 1: young, lean, abrupt onset, prone to ketoacidosis
Type 2: adult, obese, insidious onset, ketosis uncommon
Type 1 needs insulin; type 2 managed by lifestyle, oral agents and insulin as needed
questions.explanation: The difference lies in the cause of insulin lack: immune destruction in type 1 versus resistance with failing compensation in type 2. This explains the differences in presentation, ketosis and treatment.

questions.stem: Describe the microvascular and macrovascular complications of diabetes and the mechanisms by which chronic hyperglycaemia causes them.
markingGuide: Mechanisms: advanced glycation end-products, polyol pathway, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction
Nephropathy: basement membrane thickening, Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, albuminuria progressing to renal failure
Neuropathy: distal sensory loss, autonomic dysfunction
Macrovascular: accelerated atherosclerosis causing ischaemic heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease
Diabetic foot from combined neuropathy and ischaemia
questions.explanation: Hyperglycaemia injures the endothelium and basement membrane of small vessels and accelerates atherosclerosis in large ones. Control of glucose, blood pressure and lipids reduces both categories.

questions.stem: Explain the pathophysiology of diabetic ketoacidosis, including why serum potassium may be normal or high despite total body depletion, and outline the principles of initial management.
markingGuide: Severe insulin deficiency with raised glucagon and other counter-regulatory hormones
Unrestrained lipolysis, hepatic ketogenesis, ketone acids cause high anion gap metabolic acidosis
Hyperglycaemia causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration; Kussmaul breathing compensates
Potassium shifts out of cells because of acidosis and insulin lack while urinary losses deplete total body potassium
Management: intravenous fluids first, fixed-rate intravenous insulin, potassium monitoring and replacement
Identify and treat the precipitant such as infection or missed insulin
questions.explanation: Lack of insulin allows fat breakdown and ketone production, while osmotic diuresis depletes fluid and electrolytes. Insulin treatment lowers serum potassium as it moves back into cells, so potassium must be monitored and replaced.
